material.mattext: <!--RsQ_001-->When planning persuasive messages, do all of the following except …
build your credibility and present your proposal at the same time
use simple language to avoid suspicions of fantastic claims and emotional manipulation
identify your sources, especially if your audience already respects those sources
persuade with narratives, rather than trying to coerce with high-pressure tactics
<!--RsQ_002-->If you aim to change someone's attitudes, beliefs, or actions, it is vital to understand their ________, the combination of forces that drive people to satisfy their needs.
satisfaction quotient
concerns
personality
motivation
<!--RsQ_003-->A message that attempts to change an audience's attitudes, beliefs, or actions is a ________ message.
routine
negative
persuasive
positive
<!--RsQ_004-->Why are persuasive messages more difficult to write than routine messages?
Because they necessarily involve getting people to act against their own best interests
Because they invariably convey negative news to the audience
Because they are always unethical, and often illegal, to use
Because they ask audiences to give something of value or take substantial action
<!--RsQ_005-->The first task in planning persuasive messages is to …
gather information
select the right medium
organize your information
analyze the situation
<!--RsQ_006-->The demographics of a group of individuals can include information about their …
personalities
attitudes
education
lifestyles
<!--RsQ_007-->Information about the personality, attitudes, lifestyle, and other psychological characteristics of a group of individuals constitutes their …
psychographics
demographics
psychogenesis
psychogeography
<!--RsQ_008-->To improve your credibility, it is important to establish common ground because it will help your audience to …
see both sides of the issue
identify with you
be objective
do all of the above
<!--RsQ_009-->The most effective main idea for persuasive messages is …
have one thing in common
an emotional appeal
an analysis of the situation
a money-back guarantee
<!--RsQ_010-->Which of the following is true about organizing your information for persuasive messages?
Persuasive messages should be about you, the sender, and not about the receiver.
Persuasive messages should have as wide a scope as possible.
Most persuasive messages use the direct approach.
When you have a close relationship with your audience and the message is welcome, the direct approach can be effective.
<!--RsQ_011-->Using an indirect approach in persuasive messages involves …
presenting a problem without suggesting a solution
explaining reasons and building interest before asking for a decision or action
avoiding attention-grabbing statements in the introduction
merely implying the purpose of the message, without stating it clearly

<!--RsQ_012-->You are the President of the Literary Club of your college and are writing a letter to a famous writer requesting him to grant you an appointment to interview him for the Club's journal. How would you go about organizing the information in your persuasive message?
You would first explain your reasons and build interest before asking for a decision or for action.
You would state the purpose of your message in the first line and then build your case.
You would only imply the purpose of your message and not state it clearly to avoid being perceived as pushy.
You would present your problem but avoid suggesting a solution, thus showing respect for the receiver.
<!--RsQ_013-->When writing a persuasive message, …
imply how the audience has made poor choices in the past
be forthright and direct regardless of the cultural context
use complex language to show the audience you know what you are talking about
persuade with logic, evidence, and compelling narratives
<!--RsQ_014-->To establish your credibility when persuading a hostile or skeptical audience, you should do all of the following except …
use jargon and technical terms
name your sources
establish common ground with the audience
provide objective evidence for the claims and promises you make
<!--RsQ_015-->Which of the following terms stands for the first phase in the AIDA model of organizing persuasive messages?
Attention
Action
Analysis
Assessment
<!--RsQ_016-->Which of the following terms stands for the second phase in the AIDA model of organizing persuasive messages?
Inquiry
Investment
Information
Interest
<!--RsQ_017-->Which of the following terms stands for the third phase in the AIDA model of organizing persuasive messages?
Defend
Desire
Design
Demonstrate

<!--RsQ_027-->________ is an essential element of persuasion. If people don't believe in you, they won't believe in what you're promoting
Trust
<!--RsQ_028-->The attempt to change an audience's attitudes, beliefs, or actions is ________.
persuasion
<!--RsQ_029-->Information about the age, gender, occupation, income, education, and other quantifiable characteristics of your audience is called ________.
demographics
<!--RsQ_030-->Information about the personality, attitudes, lifestyle, and other psychological characteristics of an individual is called ________.

<!--RsQ_031-->Your ________ is your capability of being believed because you are reliable and worthy of confidence.
credibility
<!--RsQ_032-->With employees, especially if the information is neutral, you should choose the ________ approach.

<!--RsQ_033-->________ language usually happens naturally with persuasive messages because you are promoting an idea or a product you believe in.

<!--RsQ_034-->Discuss why it's important to understand cultural expectations when writing persuasive messages and include examples related to Indigenous Peoples and organizations.

Be sure to understand cultural expectations as well. For example, a message that seems forthright and direct in a low-context culture might seem brash and intrusive in a high-context culture. For example, when corresponding with Indigenous organizations, Indigenous Peoples will often try to establish a relationship right away by the tone of the email. This includes signing off in their Indigenous language and being clear about who they are, where they are from, and any community or nation affiliations. Establishing a relationship before you try to persuade the audience to help establish credibility. Having awareness of how to address Indigenous Peoples is very important Are you corresponding with an urban Indigenous group where the term "Indigenous" is applicable, or is it a specific First Nation that you are writing to? If the latter, what nation is it and what territory do they belong to? Being as specific as possible is a sign of respect and shows you have done your research. A useful resource when corresponding with Indigenous Peoples is the University of British Columbia's Indigenous Peoples: Language Guidelines.
<!--RsQ_035-->Describe two key steps when analyzing your audience for a persuasive message.

1. Gauge your audience's needs. What are their needs? How might they resist? What does the decision maker consider the most important issue? 2. Consider cultural differences. Persuasion is different in different cultures. Be sure you understand what is an appropriate approach in a different culture.

<!--RsQ_037-->When your AIDA message uses the indirect approach and is delivered by memo or email, your subject line should …

<!--RsQ_038-->Which of the following is true about the use of the AIDA model in organizing persuasive messages?
AIDA is a unidirectional method that essentially talks at audiences, not with them.
The AIDA model can only use the indirect approach to persuasive messages.
AIDA is especially useful for building a mutually beneficial, long-term relationship with the audience.
The AIDA model is tailor-made for using the direct approach in persuasive messages.
<!--RsQ_039-->Which of the following approaches is more compatible with persuasive messages for today's social media?
Conversational approach
AIDA approach
Unidirectional approach
Formal approach
<!--RsQ_040-->Emotional and logical appeals work together by …
allowing the audience to choose the appeal that will be most effective
providing rational support for an idea that an audience has already emotionally accepted
manipulating the audience into focusing on the emotional issues while ignoring the logical elements
doing all of the above
<!--RsQ_041-->An analogy lets you …
reason from specific evidence to a general conclusion
reason from one specific evidence to another specific evidence
reason from a generalization to a specific conclusion
do all of the above

<!--RsQ_042-->If you used the results of a taste test in which many individuals preferred your product over the competitor's to persuade others to buy your product, what kind of approach would you be using?
Induction
Analogy
Deduction
A combination of all three
<!--RsQ_043-->Which of the following is an example of an analogy?
All employees have health coverage. Therefore, since Tom is an employee, he must have health coverage.
Our office operates like a wolf pack with one Alpha male on top and everyone else answering to him.
The results of this survey showed that people like our product more than our competitor's product.

<!--RsQ_044-->Which of the following uses a deductive approach to persuasion?

<!--RsQ_045-->Which of the following is true about the use of emotional and logical appeals in persuasive messages?

<!--RsQ_046-->When using an analogy to create logical appeal, you …

The results of this survey showed that people like our product more than our competitor's product.

<!--RsQ_050-->In a bid to persuade consumers to buy your product, you quote the results of a taste test in which most individuals preferred your product over the competitor's. Which kind of reasoning device are you using in this case?

<!--RsQ_051-->"Our profits were up by 10 percent last quarter. Employee turnover has been cut by almost half from last year. Last, but not the least, our market share has increased by 15 percent over the past 9 months. Considering these figures, we can safely say that our short-term growth strategy has been a great success." Identify the reasoning method used in this message to create logical appeal.

<!--RsQ_053-->Which of the following statements uses a deductive approach to persuasion?

<!--RsQ_054-->"It is widely believed that the economy is now well on its way to recovery. Therefore, it is only a matter of time before our company also sees a turnaround." This message uses the reasoning method of ________ to create logical appeal.

<!--RsQ_055-->"You can rely on us to deliver on our promises because we are completely trustworthy." What is the best criticism for this statement?

<!--RsQ_056-->Which of the following is a guideline for avoiding faulty logic in a persuasive message?
You should be able to isolate the impact of a specific factor before assuming that it's the cause of whatever effect you're discussing.
You should try to support your claim by restating it in different words.
You should try to attack your opponent's character, not the argument your opponent is making.
You should try to reduce a complex situation to a simple "either/or" statement if the situation isn't that simple or clear-cut.

<!--RsQ_057-->"Shortly after Annie's Craft Store advertised in 'The Ridgewood Chronicle,' their sales went up by 10 percent." Which of the following facts, if true, would prove the cause-and-effect relationship implied in this message?

<!--RsQ_060-->Which of the following is a common mistake made when developing persuasive arguments?

material.mattext: <!--RsQ_065-->Most persuasive messages use a combination of emotional and logical appeals.
True
False
<!--RsQ_066-->The four-step plan for writing persuasive messages is called the ________ plan.
AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action)
<!--RsQ_067-->A(n) ________ appeal calls on human reason.
logical
<!--RsQ_068-->A(n) ________ appeal is aimed at your audience's feelings and sympathies.
emotional
<!--RsQ_069-->Many marketing and sales messages rely heavily on emotional appeals, but most persuasive business messages rely more on ________.
logic
<!--RsQ_070-->When you use specific evidence to support a general conclusion, the type of persuasive reasoning you are using is called ________.
induction
<!--RsQ_071-->Explain when you should use an emotional versus a logical appeal to persuade an audience.

Most persuasion uses a combination of both emotional and persuasive appeals. Often people need to find rational support for an attitude they have already accepted emotionally.
Emotional appeals are better when persuading someone to buy a product or to get emotionally involved by joining a cause or making a donation. Emotional appeals are usually better for less significant decisions and for audiences who already are on your side. Logical appeals are best when you are persuading someone to accept a complex idea, take a serious step, or make an important decision.
<!--RsQ_072-->Describe the three main types of logical appeals.
1. Analogy-using comparisons to persuade. 2. Induction-reasoning from specific evidence to a general conclusion. 3. Deduction-reasoning from a generalization to a specific conclusion.
Describe the four steps of the AIDA model for persuasive messages.

The AIDA model organizes your presentation into four phases:

  1. Attention: Your first objective is to encourage your audience to want to hear about your problem, idea, or new product-whatever your main idea is. Be sure to find some common ground on which to build your case.
  2. Interest: Provide additional details that prompt audience members to imagine how the solution might benefit them.
  3. Desire: Help audience members embrace your idea by explaining how the change will benefit them and answering potential objections.
  4. Action: Suggest the specific action you want your audience to take. Include a deadline, when applicable.

<!--RsQ_074-->What guidelines should be remembered when developing the subject line of your AIDA message that uses the indirect approach and is delivered by memo or email? Rewrite the following email subject line following these guidelines: "Rejection of your proposal for a four-day work week"

When your AIDA message uses the indirect approach and is delivered by memo or email, keep in mind that your subject line usually catches your reader's eye first. Your challenge is to make it interesting and relevant enough to capture the reader's attention without revealing your main idea. If you put your request in the subject line, you're likely to get a quick "no" before you've had a chance to present your arguments. Therefore, the above line can be rewritten as: "Decision on four-day workweek proposal."

As CEO of your company, you are drafting an email to persuade your managers of the need to minimize wastage of paper, power, and other resources in order to reduce the company's carbon footprint. What format would you choose to convey this message and why? Would you use the direct approach or the indirect approach in organizing this message? Justify your choice. Draft the message using your chosen format and approach.

Answers can vary as long as they are justified. Most answers will reflect the following:
The use of the AIDA model for developing this message is appropriate since this model is well-suited to persuasive messages that request for a specific action be taken. When you have a close relationship with your audience, and the message is welcome or at least neutral, the direct approach can be effective. The choice between the direct and indirect approaches for persuasive business messages is also influenced by the extent of your authority, expertise, or power in an organization. Since, in this case, the writer is the CEO of the organization and is communicating neutral news to his employees, the direct approach can be used.

When the AIDA model is used with the direct approach, the main idea must be used as an attention-getter, interest should be built with arguments, desire created with evidence, and the main idea should be emphasized in the action phase with the specific action you want your audience to take.

Subject: Seeking your cooperation in reducing the company's carbon footprint
As part of the sustainability initiatives undertaken by the company, I request all our employees to contribute to our efforts to reduce our company's carbon footprint. These environmental initiatives are vital not only for ensuring a safe future for the planet, but also for our company's long-term profitability. Some of Canada's oldest and most profitable companies have been built on a philosophy of practicing corporate social responsibility. Our company has now made sustainability the core of its mission and purpose. You can help us achieve our environmental goals by doing a few simple things like minimizing paper wastage by encouraging employees to use email and soft copies of documents, turning off the lights, bringing a reusable lunch box and bottle of water from home, and carpooling to work.

We have planned several events and workshops to increase awareness about this issue and the department with the lowest relative resource consumption will be recognized and rewarded. To learn more about what you can do to help call our Environment Officer Megan Tanner at 416-444-1234, or visit sustainabilityatwork.com.

How would you increase the emotional appeal of the following persuasive message?
"Our soup kitchen provides food to over a hundred homeless people every day. We get no funds for this from the government, and our funding comes exclusively from private individuals and corporations. Please consider contributing time and/or money to our group to help us run these soup kitchens. To make a contribution call 416-123-4567."

(Answers will vary.) The answer should contain words or phrases that call on feelings or audience sympathies. This can be achieved by using words such as freedom, success, prestige, compassion, free, and comfort. Such words put your audience in a certain frame of mind and help people accept your message.

Our soup kitchen is a refuge from cold and hunger for over a hundred homeless people every day. We get no funds for this service from the government and are completely dependent on contributions from corporations and individuals such as you. We pride ourselves on being a community that takes care of its weakest. So, please donate your time and/or money to this worthy cause. To pledge your support call 1-800-123-4567.
<!--RsQ_077-->When putting together persuasive arguments, what common mistakes should you avoid?

Using a hard sell.
Resisting compromise.
Relying solely on great arguments.
Assuming that persuasion is a one-shot effort.
Resorting to deception or other unethical behaviours.
<!--RsQ_078-->A persuasive claim should close …
by clearly indicating how denial of the claim will lead to unfavorable consequences for the individual or organization
on a positive note that reflects how a successful resolution of the situation will repair or maintain a mutually beneficial working relationship
with a sincere apology that acknowledges the trouble caused to the reader due to the claim
by outlining the problem and continuing by reviewing what has been done about it so far
<!--RsQ_079-->Which of the following is true of persuasive requests for action?
They should always use the direct approach.
They must begin with a request for some specific action.
The suggested course of action in these messages should be as easy to follow as possible.
They should avoid specifying the action required; leave the decision to the audience.

<!--RsQ_080-->Adelphia Technologies has recently launched an "I am an Adelphian" campaign that uses posters and lectures to educate employees about the importance and advantages of having a diverse workforce. What type of persuasive business message does this constitute?
Persuasive requests for action
Persuasive presentation of ideas
Persuasive requests for proposal
Persuasive claims
<!--RsQ_081-->Persuasive presentations of ideas are made in situations where you …
simply want to change attitudes or beliefs about a particular topic
wish to influence readers to take a particular course of action
seek to influence the reader to make a decision in your favor
want to present your proposals so as to gain the approval of the audience
<!--RsQ_082-->A good persuasive claim should …
always include a sincere apology for the trouble caused to the receiver
avoid wasting the receiver's time by reviewing the case in the message
be specific about how one would like to see the situation resolved
assume that the recipient already has information about the case
<!--RsQ_083-->An effective persuasive claim should avoid …
reviewing the facts of the case
using a complaining tone
being specific about how the problem should be resolved
closing on a positive note
<!--RsQ_084-->In a persuasive claim, it is important to …
avoid spelling out the desired resolution to the problem
close on a threat to terminate the relationship if the case is not resolved
avoid mentioning how the organization or individual is responsible for the problem
give your reader a good reason for granting your claim
<!--RsQ_085-->In a claim letter, the opening should …
specify a deadline for action
clearly indicate how denial of the claim will lead to unfavorable consequences for the individual or organization
outline the problem
reflect how a successful resolution of the situation will repair or maintain a mutually beneficial working relationship
<!--RsQ_086-->Marketing messages …
encourage potential buyers to make a purchase decision then and there
are synonymous with sales messages
focus on such tasks as introducing new brands to the public and providing product information
do not follow the AIDA model
<!--RsQ_087-->Sales messages …
usher potential buyers through the purchasing process without asking them to make an immediate decision
focus on such tasks as introducing new brands to the public and reminding buyers that a particular product is available
encourage customers to seek more information about a product
encourage potential buyers to make a purchase decision then and there
<!--RsQ_088-->Which of the following persuasive messages would constitute a sales message?
A message introducing a new cell phone to potential customers
A message educating potential customers about the benefits of a new cell phone
A message requesting potential customers place an order for a cell phone
A message reminding potential customers that a particular cell phone is available
<!--RsQ_089-->Given below are the closing statements of some persuasive messages. Judging from the call to action made in each, which one of these constitutes a sales message?
To know more about this product, please visit our website at akme/new.com.
To order this product, call 1-800-345-1234 or visit our online store at akme/store.com.
To receive a free product demo, call Alex at 1-800-345-1234, or email him at alex@akme.com.
To receive a free trial pack, visit our website at akme/new.com.
<!--RsQ_090-->In marketing and sales messages, what is the primary difference between selling points and benefits?
Selling points are ethical to use whereas benefits are not.
Selling points focus on the user rather than the product.
Selling points focus on the product rather than the user.
Selling points are unethical to use whereas benefits are not.

What are the guidelines for developing an effective persuasive claim?

The key ingredients of a good persuasive claim are a complete and specific review of the facts and a confident and positive tone. Remember that you have the right to be satisfied with every transaction. Begin persuasive claims by outlining the problem and continue by reviewing what has been done about it so far, if anything. The recipient might be juggling numerous claims and other demands on his or her attention, so be clear, calm, and complete when presenting your case. Be specific about how you would like to see the situation resolved.

Next, give your reader a good reason for granting your claim. Show how the individual or organization is responsible for the problem and appeal to your reader's sense of fair play, goodwill, or moral responsibility. Explain how you feel about the problem but don't get carried away, don't complain too much, and don't make threats. People generally respond most favourably to requests that are both calm and reasonable. Close on a positive note that reflects how a successful resolution of the situation will repair or maintain a mutually beneficial working relationship.
What are the guidelines for developing an effective persuasive request for action?

The bulk of your persuasive business messages will involve requests for action. In some cases, your request will be anticipated, so the direct approach is fine (refer to Figure 9.5). In others, you'll need to introduce your intention indirectly, and the AIDA model or a similar approach is ideal for this purpose (refer to Figure 9.6).

Open with an attention-getting device and show readers that you understand their concerns. Use the interest and desire sections of your message to demonstrate the need or reason for making such a request and to cover the facts, figures, and benefits of taking action and any history or experience that will enhance your appeal. Your goals are (1) to gain credibility (for yourself and your request) and (2) to make your readers believe that helping you will indeed help solve a significant problem. Close with a request for some specific action and make that course.
<!--RsQ_107-->What are the guidelines for developing an effective persuasive presentation of ideas?

You may encounter situations in which you simply want to change attitudes or beliefs about a particular topic, without asking the audience to decide or do anything-at least not yet. The goal of your first message might be nothing more than convincing your audience to re-examine long-held opinions or admit the possibility of new ways of thinking.

<!--RsQ_164-->Briefly explain the difference between selling points and benefits, giving an example of each.

Selling points are the most attractive features of an idea or product. Benefits are the particular advantages that readers will realize from those features. In other words, selling points focus on what the product does. Benefits focus on the user experiences or gains. The fact that a notebook computer comes with a fingerprint recognition device is a selling point, but the security the buyer will enjoy because of the device is a benefit.
<!--RsQ_165-->Describe ways in which you can minimize the importance of price in a sales letter. Also outline ways in which you can address audience objections to the price of your product.

If you wish to downplay the price in your sales or marketing message, you can leave out any mention of the price or place it in a less important location in the letter, near the end or mid-paragraph after you have described the benefits and selling points. Whenever price is likely to cause an objection, look for ways to increase the perceived value of the purchase and decrease the perceived cost. You can compare the price to some other product or activity in an attempt to make the price of your product seem small and affordable in comparison. You can also compare the price to the potential costs of not buying the product.
<!--RsQ_166-->List and describe the four strategies for creating a sales message.

1. Determining selling points and benefits: Know how your product's selling points benefit your audience. 2. Use action terms: Use action words and colourful language to convey a dynamic image. 3. Talking about price: Carefully consider how important the price will be to your audience. 4. Supporting your claim: You have to prove what you have claimed about your product. This might include samples, brochures, testimonials, scientific studies, guarantees, etc. Try to anticipate every question your audience may have.

Outline at least four ethical and legal aspects that must be considered when developing marketing and sales messages.

1. Marketing and sales messages must be truthful and nondeceptive. Failing to include important information is considered deceptive.
  2. You must back up your claims with evidence. You must still be able to support your claims with objective evidence such as a survey or scientific study. For instance, if you claim that your food product lowers cholesterol, you must have scientific evidence to support that claim.
  3. "Bait and switch" advertising is illegal. Trying to attract buyers by advertising a product that you don't intend to sell-and then trying to sell them another (and usually more expensive) product-is illegal.
  4. To maintain the highest standards of business ethics, always demonstrate the "you" attitude by showing honest concern for your audience's needs and interests.
  5. Before you launch a marketing or sales campaign, make sure you're up to date on the latest regulations affecting spam (or unsolicited bulk email), customer privacy, and data security.

In Alberta, there is a ban on all retail tobacco displays (power walls). Do you agree that the marketing of some products, for example those that carry health risks, should be restricted? Explain your answer and cite examples for support.

(responses will vary)
YES, I agree that the marketing of some products should be restricted. "The tobacco industry continues to target Alberta's youth through candy and fruit flavoured products, price discounts, colourful packaging, and slim-style cigarettes. For example, spit tobacco is not labelled or regulated to the same standard as other tobacco products and contains candy flavours that appeal to youth. Tobacco sales to minors' regulations are needed to help counter these objectionable marketing practices. Such laws will prevent more kids from falling prey to tobacco companies. The tobacco industry claims that it is supporting programs that reduce tobacco sales to minors. However, these programs place the primary responsibility on adolescents rather than retailers and they have been proven ineffective. For example, the signage for the Operation ID program places the onus on youth to produce ID rather than urging retailers to demand it. Alberta can do a better job of protecting kids from the predatory marketing practices of the tobacco industry. Alberta kids deserve first-class protection from the deadly and addictive consequences of tobacco use." See more at: http://www.smokefreealberta.com/issues/sales-to-minors.html#sthash.kooIh03C.dpuf

NO, I disagree that the marketing of some products should be restricted unless, of course, the product is illegal. Otherwise, in the case of legal products such as tobacco and alcohol, and even fast food, it is up to the consumer to make an informed choice about whether she or he will buy the product. We live in a free-market society where companies have the right to both advertise and sell their products. In the case of minors, it is the parents' responsibility to educate their children on making good decisions and not buying or using products, such as tobacco and alcohol, when they are underage. Once we start restrictive practices within marketing, where does it end? Will only "healthy" products be advertised? Who gets to make these decisions? Let's allow savvy consumers to decide what they want to buy, or not.
